Reviewer 2:
Major points:
1. Particularly, overexpression of STING in some vital experiments raise significant
doubt about the interpretation of the results since the results may be based on a non-
physiological model system with artefacts affecting the results. The fluorescence
microscopy imaging data need to be improved. The imaging data in this paper will also
be very much improved to obtain more secure conclusions if the authors used
correlative light and electron microscopy to determine the fate of STING from the Golgi
to the lysosome. Another improvement would be to use Halo-tagged STING to follow
the lysosomal turnover of STING in a quantitative manner to enable comparison with
other pathways like ESCRT-dependent microautophagy (ref. 11) and STING-dependent
macroautophagy.
We thank the reviewer for these comments and agree that the imaging data required
improvement. To this end, we generated HeLa cells stably expressing STING-eGFP
and have repeated all the imaging experiments. Our new data, which is consistent with
our previous data, indicate an impairment in STING trafficking to recycling endosomes
and lysosomes in TAX1BP1 knockout cells. Correlative light and electron microscopy is
an excellent suggestion, but we did not perform the experiment because the new and
improved imaging data provided strong evidence of an impairment in STING trafficking
from the Golgi to lysosomes in the absence of TAX1BP1. As recommended, we have
performed STING degradation assays using THP-1 cells stably expressing STING-
eGFP. Our new quantitative flow cytometry data (Fig. 4A-E) provides additional
evidence that TAX1BP1 is involved in STING degradation.
2. As a continuation of point 1: How important is this pathway described here relative to
ESCRT-dependent degradation of STING by microautophagy? Can the authors
determine the fraction of STING that is degraded by the Golgi-fragmentation pathway
aided by TAX1BP1? What about KO of p62 and other SLRs to determine if they have a
role together with TAX1BP1?
These are excellent points raised by the reviewer. Our new data indicates that STING
interaction with the ESCRT-0 protein HGS is diminished in the absence of TAX1BP1
(Fig. 4F-H). Furthermore, knockdown of TSG101, a core component of the ESCRT-0
complex significantly inhibits STING degradation (Fig. 4C-E). However, knockdown of
TSG101 together with TAX1BP1 knockout completely impairs STING degradation (Fig.
4C-E). These data suggest that TAX1BP1 mediates STING degradation through both
ESCRT-dependent and independent mechanisms. Although STING+ vesicles that have
egressed from the Golgi are degraded by microautophagy, STING-induced Golgiphagy
appears to be independent of macroautophagy and microautophagy. These data are
shown in Supplementary Fig. 9. Since LC3 lipidation is unimpaired in TAX1BP1 KO
macrophages treated with diABZI, we suspect that STING degradation by Golgiphagy
occurs through FIP200-independent noncanonical autophagy. We have also generated
p62/SQSTM1 knockout THP-1 cells and showed that both STING and Golgi
degradation are impaired (Fig. 8F). A previous study showed that p62 colocalizes with
both STING and HGS (Gentili et al. Nat. Comm. 2023; PMID: 36739287). Together, our
data suggests that both TAX1BP1 and p62 are involved in STING-induced Golgiphagy
and ESCRT-mediated degradation of STING by microautophagy. Regarding other
SLRs, a recent study from the Youle lab found that TNIP1 and other autophagy
receptors including p62, NBR1, NDP52, TAX1BP1 and OPTN all associate with STING-
induced ubiquitin and LC3+ vesicles (Bunker et al. 2025 BioRxiv). Future studies are
needed to assess other SLRs for potential roles in STING-induced Golgiphagy.
3. Could it be that TAX1BP1 is primarily important here as an autophagy receptor for
degradation of fragmented Golgi and that STING is simply degraded as a bystander?
Do the authors provoke Golgi fragmentation and thereby TAX1BP1-dependent
Golgiphagy by overexpressing STING too much?
Our new data indicate that TAX1BP1 directly interacts with STING and links STING to
the ESCRT machinery (Figs. 4, 5). This suggests that STING is not degraded as a
bystander but is specifically targeted for degradation by TAX1BP1. TAX1BP1 appears
to serve as an autophagy receptor for fragmented Golgi after STING activation but may
also promote STING degradation of STING vesicles that have egressed from the Golgi
to traffic to lysosomes. New experiments were repeated with cells stably expressing
STING to avoid potential artifacts from STING transient overexpression. Golgi
fragmentation is also observed by transmission electron microscopy using primary WT
and Tax1bp1–/– macrophages (Fig. 9) again suggesting that STING-induced Golgi
fragmentation is not caused by overexpression artifacts.
4. KO of TAX1BP1 in human monocytic THP-1 cells led to increased resistance to
Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection and increased expression of mRNAs for
Ifn-b, Ifna4, Mx1, Isg15 and Irf7 (Fig. 2B, D-G). However, I find the increase in the IFN-b
protein level to be relatively small in Fig.2C with no change at 12h and a small increase
at 24h. Can the authors comment on this?
The reviewer raises a good point about the observed upregulation in HSV-induced IFN-
beta production in TAX1BP1-KO THP-1 cells (Fig. 2). While there are statistically
significant differences at some of the time points, we don’t know the reason why some
of the changes are relatively small. We suspect it could be due to the influence of HSV-
1-encoded antagonists of STING such as UL38.
5. In Figure 3A and -B, the blots for pTBK1 (S172), pIRF3 (S396), pSTING (S366) as
well as pIKKalpha/beta (S176/180 and pIkBalpha (S32/36) need quantifications with
statistics.
Done as requested. The pTBK1, pIRF3, pSTING and pIKK bands were quantified from
three independent experiments. We removed the pIkBa blots since our previous
antibody was depleted and a new antibody that originated from a different lot no longer
worked.
6. Importantly, also the total levels of STING should be quantified in Fig. 3A and 3B
from the blots shown. From just visual inspection there does not seem to be a profound
turnover of STING, but this may of course be balanced by increased expression of
STING?
The experiments were repeated, and STING bands were quantified from three
independent experiments. See Fig. 3A-L.
7. Lines 168-169: The authors write that “However, in Tax1bp1–/– BMDMs treated with
diABZI, STING degradation was largely impaired (Fig. 3C).” From the top blot in Figure
3C this clearly seems an overstatement and the authors need to quantify the STING
levels from the experiments in Fig. 3C.
The STING bands were quantified by densitometry. We have also added new
quantitative flow cytometry STING degradation assays in Fig. 4 in the manuscript that
provides additional support for TAX1BP1 in STING degradation.
8. In Fig. 4A the band of IPed TAX1BP1 (IPed with a TAX1BP1 antibody) migrates
below the 75 kDa MW marker while the band of TAX1BP1 IPed with STING (IPed with a
STING antibody) migrates clearly above the 75 kDa MW marker. How can the authors
explain these seemingly very different molecular weights of TAX1BP1 observed in the
two IP experiments?
We have repeated the STING-TAX1BP1 co-IP assay and IPed TAX1BP1 in both STING
and TAX1BP1 immunoprecipitates now migrates above the 75 kDa band as expected.
9. Does TAX1BP1 bind directly to STING? Importantly, the authors need to show that
STING and TAX1BP1 can directly interact with each other. IP from cells and PLA
suggest that STING and TAX1BP1 may be in a complex but assays for direct
interactions are needed such as for example GST pulldowns of recombinant proteins
and/or bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays.
We have performed a nanoBiT complementation assay to demonstrate a direct
interaction between TAX1BP1 and STING. The new data is shown in Fig. 5F, G.
10. The imaging shown in Figure 4D needs quantifications of colocalizations and an
estimate of how relevant the fluorescence signal distributions shown are as only single
cells are shown in the top and bottom panels.
Quantification of the colocalization is now provided in the new Fig. 5E.
11. The resolution of the images in Fig 4D should be significantly improved. This is
especially important for the lower panel diABZI (2h). See for example the imaging
shown in reference 11 (Kuchitsu et al. 2023).
We have repeated the immunofluorescence experiments (new Fig. 5D) and the
resolution is now significantly improved.
12. The quality and resolution of the imaging shown in Fig. 5A and D need to be
improved.
We have repeated the immunofluorescence experiments and the resolution is now
significantly improved.
13 (Related to point 1 and 3). Importantly, the overexpression of STING affects the
experiment a lot since Golgi looks completely fragmented in the TGN46 staining in Fig
5A. The impression that STING is degraded as a bystander by TAX1BP1 mediated
Golgiphagy caused by a non-physiological level of STING due to overexpression
becomes strong from looking at these data.
This is a valid concern. In the revised manuscript, we generated HeLa cells stably
expressing STING-eGFP and repeated the immunofluorescence experiments.
Importantly, we have confirmed STING-induced Golgi fragmentation using Golgin-97
staining as well as using a newly generated Golgiphagy reporter (Fig. 8C, D;
Supplementary Fig. 8D, E).
14. (Related to 1, 3 and 13). In Fig.7C STING is highly overexpressed completely
compromising the imaging data making it impossible to trust the conclusions made.
We have repeated the immunofluorescence experiments with HeLa cells stably
expressing STING-eGFP and the resolution is now significantly improved.
15. The imaging data in Supplementary Figure 7B are far from publication quality and
the experiments need quantification of the number of red only dots per cells and fraction
of red to yellow dots.
We agree and have modified the Golgiphagy reporter with a minimal Golgi targeting
motif (FLWRIFCFRK) as previously reported (Kitta et al. EMBO J. 2024; PMID
38822137). Instead of THP-1 cells, new experiments were performed in control and
TAX1BP1-KO HeLa cells stably expressing the Golgiphagy reporter. The new images
are significantly improved and shown in Fig. 8C, D and Supplementary Fig. 8D, E.
Quantification of mCherry+GFP– puncta is provided as described in Kitta et al. EMBO J.
We also validated the Golgiphagy reporter and showed colocalization of red and green
perinuclear fluorescence intensity with a Golgi marker (Supplementary Fig. 8E). The
data indicate that TAX1BP1 is required for STING-induced Golgiphagy and likely
functions as a Golgiphagy receptor for STING-induced fragmented Golgi.
Minor comments:
Line 56 in the Introduction: The authors refer to the “ULK-Beclin kinase complex”. This
needs to be corrected since these are two complexes with the ULK1/2 kinase complex
being distinct from the PI3K class III complex 1 containing Beclin1.
Done
Reviewer 3:
The authors identified a novel mechanism by which TAX1BP1 regulates anti-viral
response pathways through STING inhibition. This regulatory mechanism involves
TAX1BP1 facilitating the degradation of STING via Golgi autophagy (Golgiphagy),
thereby downregulating the cGAS-STING pathway and suggesting its role in modulating
inflammatory responses. Although the negative regulation of the cGAS-STING pathway
through the Golgi is highly intriguing, there are significant gaps that need to be
addressed before accepting the authors’ claims. The primary concern is that the
suppression mechanism of the cGAS-STING pathway by TAX1BP1 appears to be
highly limited in humans or mice, making the interpretation of the data unclear. I strongly
recommend that the authors conduct a more detailed analysis in both humans and
mice.
As stated by the authors in the Introduction, TAX1BP1 has been previously shown to
inhibit IFN induction through the RLRs pathway and some TLR pathways. Therefore,
the authors should investigate whether similar phenomena are observed in TAX1BP1
KO THP-1 cells and BMDMs. At the very least, experiments using PolyIC stimulation of
RLRs, TLR stimulation with agents like LPS, and RNA virus infection experiments
should be performed. Additionally, further induction of IFN through the cGAS-STING
pathway should be conducted using TAX1BP1 KO THP-1 cells and BMDMs. The
authors’ current experiments are limited to using G3-YSD, cGAMP, and HSV-1; hence,
they should assess IFN induction through the cGAS-STING pathway using ligands
known to activate this pathway, such as PolydAdT, ISD, and several DNA viruses.
We and others have already published that TAX1BP1 inhibits type I IFN induced by
RLR and TLR signaling (see PMID: 27736772, 39193925, 17703191, 29358708,
28898289). In fact, our recent study (PMID: 39193925) directly compared poly(I:C)
stimulation versus virus infection for TAX1BP1 degradation and autophagy function. Our
focus in this manuscript is on TAX1BP1 regulation of the cGAS-STING pathway. We
have already used the cGAS agonist G3-YSD, cGAMP and HSV-1 infection in vitro. Our
results are in agreement and indicate that TAX1BP1 knockout macrophages exhibit
increased type I IFN induction in response to all these agonists. However, we have
used an additional cGAS ligand, HT-DNA, and showed increased type I IFN responses
in TAX1BP1-KO THP-1 cells (Supplementary Fig. 3). Furthermore, we have used an
additional DNA virus Ectromelia virus, a mouse poxvirus, for in vivo studies and showed
that myeloid-specific TAX1BP1 knockout mice are more resistant to Ectromelia infection
(Fig. 10). In aggregate, we have used multiple cGAS and STING agonists in this study.
Understanding the suppression mechanism of the cGAS-STING pathway by TAX1BP1
in humans and mice is crucial and reveals an extremely interesting phenomenon.
However, despite using TAX1BP1 KO THP-1 cells and BMDMs in some experiments,
not all experiments were conducted using these cells. This is insufficient as supporting
data for the authors' claims. The authors should conduct experiments using TAX1BP1
KO THP-1 cells and BMDMs in all experimental setups, and discuss each result to
comprehensively examine the suppression mechanism of the cGAS-STING pathway by
TAX1BP1 in both humans and mice.
We thank the reviewer for finding the TAX1BP1 suppression mechanism of cGAS-
STING to be extremely interesting. The reviewer raises a good point that not all
experiments were performed in TAX1BP1 knockout THP-1 cells and BMDMs. The
reasons for this are practical. We initially attempted confocal/immunofluorescence
experiments in BMDMs and THP-1 cells but found that STING staining and resolution of
the Golgi were suboptimal in these cells. Many papers, including high profile studies in
Nature, Mol. Cell and others (see PMID: 36261523, 37086726, 33201170, 39578541,
35649354) have used HeLa cells stably expressing STING-eGFP for studying STING
trafficking and localization owing to their relatively large cytoplasm and uniform
morphology.
The suppression mechanism of the cGAS-STING pathway is critical, as its breakdown
is reported to be associated with autoimmune diseases like COPA syndrome and SAVI.
Previous studies have also reported that TAX1BP1 negatively regulates IFN induction,
and the relationship between its malfunction and disease is an important issue.
Nevertheless, the authors have not provided sufficient results related to these matters,
conducting only infection experiments with TAX1BP1flox/flox LysM-Cre mice. The
authors should analyze the relationship between diseases related to the cGAS-STING
pathway and TAX1BP1 by performing scRNA-seq on samples obtained from patients.
This approach could elucidate the biological functions of TAX1BP1 more effectively.
Additionally, a comprehensive analysis using samples from patients with
neurodegenerative diseases caused by Golgi abnormalities should be conducted.
We appreciate the emphasis on disease raised by the reviewer. However, COPA
syndrome and SAVI are extremely rare diseases and we do not have access to these
patient samples or mouse models. Similarly, we do not have access to samples from
patients with neurodegenerative diseases caused by Golgi abnormalities. Although we
agree that these would be very interesting avenues to pursue, we feel that these studies
will not directly address any questions about the mechanisms by which TAX1BP1
inhibits STING and are also beyond the scope of this manuscript.
There are several errors and inconsistencies in the figure legends and the main text that
the authors should review and correct. For example, there is inconsistent terminology
between "Real-time qRT-PCR" in L104 and "qRT-PCR" in L102, and an error in L786
where "yellow arrow" should be "yellow arrowhead." Additionally, in Fig. 3A, the
comparison targets are not shown on the same membrane, making the comparison
invalid and unacceptable. Furthermore, in the case of immunofluorescence staining,
while some quantifications are provided, most figures show only a single cell in one field
of view, and many lack quantification altogether. As a solution, the authors must provide
quantitative data for all these experiments to address these issues comprehensively.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out these errors. We have fixed all the minor errors
in terminology. The experiment in Fig. 3A has been repeated and all samples were
loaded on the same gel. All immunofluorescence experiments in the manuscript were
repeated and quantification provided. We now show multiple cells in every field for
immunofluorescence experiments.
Reviewer 4:
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Reviewer 5:
In this manuscript, the authors suggested that TAX1BP1 was involved in STING
degradation and the degradation was mediated by Golgiphagy. They exploited several
approaches to address the in vivo significance, including generation of KO mice and
virus infections, and convincingly showed that TAX1BP1 was a negative regulator of
STING signalling. In contrast, the mechanistic insight of the study is weak as described
below.
The authors might find the following specific comments useful to improve the study.
Critiques:
(1) Many studies excluded the contribution of macroautophagy to STING degradation
(For example, Nature (2019) 567, 262-266, Extended Fig.6). Furthermore, recent
papers suggested that microautophagy, which does not require Atg genes and thus
isolation membrane, is the critical process that mediates STING degradation.
We thank the reviewer for raising this point and agree that macroautophagy does not
play a role in STING degradation. To address this point, we generated THP-1 cells
lacking the core autophagy gene Atg3 which is required for LC3 lipidation. ATG3
knockout cell lines were treated with diABZI to examine STING and Golgi degradation.
Indeed, our data agrees with earlier studies that macroautophagy is dispensable for
STING degradation (Supplementary Fig. 9B). Therefore, we have removed all
statements in the manuscript that macroautophagy is involved in STING degradation.
Interestingly, STING-induced Golgi degradation occurs in the absence of ATG3 and
FIP200 (Supplementary Fig. 9D), as well as TSG101 knockdown (Supplementary Fig.
9E), suggesting that STING-induced Golgiphagy occurs independently of
macroautophagy and microautophagy. We suspect it is a FIP200-independent
noncanonical autophagy pathway.
The data in Figure 3C, in which the blot of LC3 was shown, did not address which
pathway was involved in STING degradation. The authors should be cautious about that
the emergence of LC3-II does not necessarily indicate that macroautophagy is in
process. In particular in the case of STING activation, CASM (conjugation of Atg8 to
single membrane) occurs at the TGN/endosomes, which is not relevant to STING
degradation.
Therefore, the authors should test if knockout or knockdown of the Atg genes impacts
STING degradation in BMDMs.
These are excellent points raised by the reviewer. We agree that STING-induced LC3
lipidation is associated with its ion channel function and CASM. We experienced
technical issues attempting to knock out ATG proteins in BMDMs and therefore we
generated the knockouts in THP-1 cells. In the absence of ATG3 or FIP200
(Supplementary Fig. 9), STING degradation is not impaired suggesting that
microautophagy is the main pathway leading to STING degradation. To address the role
of microautophagy we knocked down the ESCRT-0 protein TSG101 and examined
STING degradation using a quantitative flow cytometry assay. The results in Fig. 4C-E
indicate that microautophagy is indeed the main pathway leading to STING degradation.
(2) The degradation of STING did not appear to be significantly affected by TAX1BP1-
KO (Figure 3). The STING becomes ubiquitinated and thus upshifted (or smeared) in
SDS-PAGE, which sometimes makes interpretation of the results difficult. This reviewer
suggests to use fluorescence protein-tagged STING to validate the degradation rate of
STING by FACS (For example, Nat Cell Biol (2023) 25, 453-466).
We thank the reviewer for this excellent suggestion. We generated THP-1 cells stably
expressing STING-eGFP and examined diABZI-induced STING degradation by flow
cytometry. TAX1BP1 knockout macrophages have a significant impairment in STING
degradation (Fig. 4A, B).
(3) In related to the critique (2), WB needs quantitation throughout the manuscript.
Done as requested
(4) In the Nat Cell Biol paper, STING was shown to move to recycling endosomes after
its exit from the Golgi/TGN, where STING becomes ubiquitinated. Therefore, the
authors should investigate carefully the site of STING arrest in TAX1BP1 KO (the Golgi
vs recycling endosomes). Also, the authors should investigate the ubiquitinated status
of STING in TAX1BP1 KO.
We performed immunofluorescence experiments to examine diABZI-induced STING
trafficking from the trans-Golgi (Golgin-97) to recycling endosomes (Transferrin
receptor) and lysosomes (LAMP2). Our data indicate that STING trafficking to recycling

assay with endogenous ubiquitin several times but were unable to get this assay to
work. We hope the reviewer appreciates the technical challenges associated with this

authors should examine if the degradation of Golgin97 requires the function of Atg

mediates STING-induced Golgiphagy.

should provide the clear mechanistic insights.

us to further improve the manuscript which we hope is now acceptable for
publication in Nature Communications. The following is a point-by-point response
to the reviewers’ comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have responded to main concerns raised and this revised manuscript is
now acceptable for publication.
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have answered all my comments and criticisms and improved the
manuscript substantially. There is still more work to be done to sort out the mechanistic
details of the microautophagy and Golgiphagy pathways implicated here. However,
given all that has been done in this paper now, I regard that as future studies which are
beyond the scope of this study.
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors make an interesting and internally consistent claim that TAX1BP1
suppresses the cGAS–STING pathway during DNA virus responses using myeloid cells.
However, there are insufficient data to fully support this claim, and we strongly
recommend more detailed analyses as follows;

RLR and TLR signaling (see PMID: 27736772, 39193925, 17703191, 29358708,

focus in this manuscript is on TAX1BP1 regulation of the cGAS-STING pathway. We
have already used the cGAS agonist G3-YSD, cGAMP and HSV-1 infection in vitro. Our
results are in agreement and indicate that TAX1BP1 knockout macrophages exhibit
increased type I IFN induction in response to all these agonists. However, we have used
an additional cGAS ligand, HT-DNA, and showed increased type I IFN responses in
TAX1BP1-KO THP-1 cells (Supplementary Fig. 3). Furthermore, we have used an
additional DNA virus Ectromelia virus, a mouse poxvirus, for in vivo studies and showed
that myeloid-specific TAX1BP1 knockout mice are more resistant to Ectromelia infection
(Fig. 10). In aggregate, we have used multiple cGAS and STING agonists in this study.”
We partially agree with the authors’ conclusions. Nonetheless, because the authors’
experiments are performed consistently in myeloid cells while many of the cited studies
rely primarily on MEFs and other non-myeloid cells, they should determine whether the
TAX1BP1-dependent suppression of the cGAS–STING pathway is a myeloid-cell-
specific phenomenon. To this end, the authors should assess IFN expression and
production after RLR and TLR pathway activation in myeloid TAX1BP1-deficient cells
such as BMDMs and THP-1.
We have performed experiments to examine RLR and TLR activation in TAX1BP1-
knockout (KO) THP-1 cells. It should be noted that we and others have already
published that TAX1BP1 restricts RLR and TLR pathways (PMID: 27736772; 39193925;
17703191; 29358708; 28898289). As expected, loss of TAX1BP1 potentiates RLR and
TLR4 activation in THP-1 cells (see data below). Control and TAX1BP1-KO THP-1 cells
were infected with VSV at an MOI of 1 and qRT-PCR was performed to examine the
induction of Ifn and Il6 mRNAs. There was more Ifn and Il6 at 8h of VSV infection in
TAX1BP1-KO THP-1 cells (see below). We also treated control and TAX1BP1-KO THP-
1 cells with LPS (500 ng) and examined Ifn and Il6 mRNAs by qRT-PCR. There was
significantly more Ifn and Il6 in LPS-treated TAX1BP1-KO THP-1 cells. This data was
not included in the revised manuscript because the cGAS-STING pathway is the focus
of this study and we intend to use this data in a future manuscript.
“We thank the reviewer for finding the TAX1BP1 suppression mechanism of
cGASSTING to be extremely interesting. The reviewer raises a good point that not all
experiments were performed in TAX1BP1 knockout THP-1 cells and BMDMs. The
reasons for this are practical. We initially attempted confocal/immunofluorescence
experiments in BMDMs and THP-1 cells but found that STING staining and resolution of
the Golgi were suboptimal in these cells. Many papers, including high profile studies in
Nature, Mol. Cell and others (see PMID: 36261523, 37086726, 33201170, 39578541,
35649354) have used HeLa cells stably expressing STING-eGFP for studying STING
trafficking and localization owing to their relatively large cytoplasm and uniform
morphology.”
Other reviewers have likewise suggested performing confocal/immunofluorescence
experiments using BMDMs, THP-1, or other myeloid cells. The authors respond that
“STING staining and resolution of the Golgi were suboptimal in these cells,” but
confocal/immunofluorescence analyses of STING and the Golgi have been performed in
numerous published studies. Therefore, the authors should carry out these
confocal/immunofluorescence experiments in the indicated myeloid cell types.
Reviewer 1 expressed a similar concern about using non-myeloid cells for imaging
studies but nevertheless was satisfied with our imaging experiments in the revised
paper using HeLa control and TAX1BP1-KO STING-eGFP cells. To confirm that the
results obtained in myeloid cells are congruent with those obtained in HeLa cells, we
examined diABZI-induced STING trafficking to the trans-Golgi in THP-1 cells stably
expressing STING-eGFP and control gRNA (control THP-1 STING-eGFP) and
TAX1BP1-KO STING-eGFP THP-1 cells. Similar to the results obtained in HeLa cells,
there was significantly more diABZI-induced STING localized to the trans-Golgi in
TAX1BP1-KO STING-eGFP THP-1 cells compared to control THP-1 STING-eGFP cells
(see data below). Therefore, we conclude that the mechanisms of STING trafficking and
regulation by TAX1BP1 are conserved in HeLa cells and myeloid cells.
“We appreciate the emphasis on disease raised by the reviewer. However, COPA
syndrome and SAVI are extremely rare diseases and we do not have access to these
patient samples or mouse models. Similarly, we do not have access to samples from
patients with neurodegenerative diseases caused by Golgi abnormalities. Although we
agree that these would be very interesting avenues to pursue, we feel that these studies
will not directly address any questions about the mechanisms by which TAX1BP1
inhibits STING and are also beyond the scope of this manuscript.”
The authors also state that “COPA syndrome and SAVI are extremely rare diseases and
we do not have access to these patient samples or mouse models.” However, multiple
patient-derived datasets are publicly available in repositories such as NCBI. The
authors should therefore discuss the relationship between TAX1BP1 and these
disorders—or with other IFN-related or Golgi-disruption-associated diseases—using
these publicly available datasets.
We have accessed publicly available datasets for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-
seq) from SAVI patients. We examined TAX1BP1, p62/SQSTM1 and NBR1 expression
in SAVI patients to determine if these key negative regulators of STING activation are
downregulated in SAVI patients. However, as seen in the volcano plot below, there are
no statistically significant differences in TAX1BP1, p62/SQSTM1 or NBR1 expression in
SAVI patients compared to controls.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors mostly addressed to the original critiques and the quality of the study has
been much improved. The elucidation of the site of STING accumulation in TAX1BP KO
cells is neat.
Major critiques:
(1) Some papers including (PMID: 36918692) showed that HGS was dispensable for
STING degradation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. Therefore, the requirement of HGS
(or HRS) for STING degradation has to be validated in their experimental settings.
There may be cell type-specific differences in HGS regulation of STING degradation. A
previous study performed in human fibroblasts (PMID: 36739287) showed that STING
degradation is indeed dependent on HGS. More relevant to our study, another group
knocked out HGS using CRISPR-Cas9 in iBMDMs, and this resulted in enhanced
STING, TBK1 and IRF3 phosphorylation and STING degradation was impaired (PMID:
37139896). Nevertheless, we attempted this experiment several times but HGS
knockdown led to significant cell death that prevented us from obtaining reliable western
blot results.
(2) Virtually, all of the ESCRT-mediated processes require VPS4a/b function. The
authors should test whether VPS4a/b KD (in addition to TSG101 KD performed in the
revision), affects Golgiphagy.
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We knocked down VPS4a and VPS4b
separately in THP-1 cells and neither had any effect on the degradation of Golgin-97.
We then combined the siRNAs for VPS4a and VPS4b and again there was no effect on
Golgin-97 degradation. This data is presented in Supplementary Fig. 9G. Together,
with our TSG101 knockdown results, we conclude that microautophagy is not involved in
STING-induced Golgi degradation.
Minor critique:
(3) It has been well established that TBK1 is not required for STING degradation.
Therefore, texts regarding the interaction between TAX1BP and TBK1 needs to be
carefully revised.
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We have toned down our conclusions from
the rescue experiment with the TAX1BP1 A114Q mutant that is impaired in binding to
both FIP200 and TBK1. This mutant is impaired in the inhibition of STING induction of
IFN and IL-6 (Supplementary Figure 7); however, we don’t know if TAX1BP1
interaction with FIP200 or TBK1 mediates suppresses STING induction of type I
interferon and cytokines. Since STING-induced Golgiphagy still occurs in the absence
of FIP200, our findings suggest that TAX1BP1 interacts with TBK1 to promote a
noncanonical form of autophagy that leads to Golgi degradation.
(4) The authors would like to examine if p62 rescue into p62-KO cells restores the
STING degradation.
We have rescued p62 expression in p62-KO THP-1 cells using a lentiviral vector and
examined STING and Golgin-97 degradation. As expected, restoration of p62 rescued
both STING and Golgin-97 degradation. This data is presented in Supplementary Fig.
9A.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The cGAS-STING pathway is a critical regulator of type I Interferon (IFN) and inflammation upon cytosolic DNA-sensing. cGAS-STING signaling termination is regulated by lysosomal-mediated degradation of STING; however, the mechanisms controlling the inhibitory targeting of STING are incompletely understood. Here, we identify the selective autophagy receptor TAX1BP1 as a negative regulator of the cGAS-STING pathway. TAX1BP1-deficient macrophages activated by cGAS or STING agonists accumulate higher-order STING aggregates, exhibit heightened STING signaling, and increased production of type I IFN and proinflammatory cytokines. Mechanistically, TAX1BP1 promotes STING degradation through microautophagy by facilitating the interaction of STING with the ESCRT-0 protein HGS. Furthermore, STING activation is associated with the swelling and fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus, and TAX1BP1 and p62/SQSTM1 are essential for the autophagic degradation of fragmented Golgi (Golgiphagy). Our findings suggest that STING activation at the Golgi is coupled to its downregulation by Golgiphagy to restrict innate immune responses.

---

## Introduction

The cGAS-STING pathway is an ancient DNA-sensing pathway critical for inflammatory responses to bacteria, DNA viruses and retroviruses1. Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) is a DNA sensor that binds double-stranded DNA and catalyzes the cyclic dinucleotide and second messenger 2’3’-cyclic GMP-AMP (2’3’-cGAMP; hereafter referred to as cGAMP), which binds to and activates Stimulator of Interferon Genes (STING) at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)2–4. STING then translocates from the ER to the Golgi via coat protein complex II (COPII) vesicles5. At the trans-Golgi, oligomerized STING activates the kinase TBK1 and transcription factor IRF3, leading to the induction of type I interferon (IFN)6.

The activation of the cGAS-STING pathway is tightly regulated to prevent overexuberant or chronic inflammation. Upon activation at the trans-Golgi, STING is targeted for degradation in lysosomes. The selective autophagy receptor p62/SQSTM1 was previously shown to promote STING degradation7; however, the underlying mechanisms are not well understood. STING also has a primordial function, inducing autophagy independent of TBK1 activation and the induction of type I IFN8,9. STING can interact with LC3 and induce autophagy dependent on ATG5 but independent of ULK1 and Beclin18. STING-induced autophagy plays a role in the clearance of viruses and DNA from the cytoplasm. Recent studies have indicated that microautophagy is the main STING degradation pathway that terminates STING signaling. STING exits the trans-Golgi network (TGN) by adaptor protein complex 1 (AP-1)-mediated sorting into clathrin-coated vesicles and is ubiquitinated by lysine 63 (K63)-linked polyubiquitin (polyUb) chains, which are sensed by the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) machinery10–13. STING vesicles are then directly encapsulated into LAMP1-positive lysosomes, resulting in STING degradation11. STING degradation is critical to prevent prolonged activation and induction of type I IFN and proinflammatory cytokines; however, the mechanisms underlying STING downregulation after its activation at the trans-Golgi are incompletely understood.

Tax1 Binding Protein 1 (TAX1BP1) was initially identified as an interacting protein of the human T-cell leukemia virus 1 (HTLV-1) Tax protein, and the NF-κB regulatory proteins A20 (also known as TNFAIP3) and TRAF614,15. TAX1BP1 was shown to inhibit NF-κB signaling by serving as an adaptor for A20 and its substrates targeted for deubiquitination16. In addition to regulating NF-κB, TAX1BP1 also inhibits the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) pathway and the induction of type I IFN triggered by RNA virus infection17,18. TAX1BP1 also blocks RLR-mediated apoptosis by interacting with MAVS and promoting its degradation19. In the absence of TAX1BP1, MAVS aggregates spontaneously form and accumulate further with RNA virus infection20. In addition, TAX1BP1 suppresses the Toll-like receptor (TLR) 3/4 pathways by targeting the adaptor TRIF for degradation21,22. TAX1BP1 inhibits NF-κB and innate immune signaling pathways to quell inflammation and prevent autoimmunity since TAX1BP1 expression was shown to be downregulated in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)23. TAX1BP1 functions as a selective autophagy receptor that contains two LC3 interaction regions (LIR) in the amino (N)-terminus and a ubiquitin binding zinc finger domain 2 (ZnF2) in the carboxy (C)-terminus24–27. TAX1BP1 detects ubiquitinated cargo via its ZnF2 domain, which is then recruited to developing autophagosomes via its LIR domains. TAX1BP1 also interacts with myosin VI, a cytoskeletal actin-based motor protein regulating vesicular transport, to induce autophagosome maturation26. Therefore, TAX1BP1 exerts multiple roles in autophagy, including cargo selection and autophagosome maturation. Although TAX1BP1 has been shown to inhibit NF-κB, RLR and TLR signaling, a potential role of TAX1BP1 in the regulation of the cGAS-STING pathway has not yet been investigated.

In this study, we identify TAX1BP1 as a negative regulator of the cGAS-STING pathway by targeting STING for degradation through autophagy of the Golgi apparatus (Golgiphagy) and ESCRT-mediated microautophagy. Loss of TAX1BP1 impairs STING degradation, leading to the accumulation of fragmented Golgi and STING aggregates and increased production of type I IFN and proinflammatory cytokines. Mice lacking TAX1BP1 in myeloid cells exhibit enhanced STING-mediated inflammatory responses and are resistant to poxvirus infection. These findings indicate that TAX1BP1 targets STING by Golgiphagy and microautophagy to limit the magnitude and duration of innate immune activation.
